show_statement: This is a show about a field getting emptier and then filling back up, and it knows it. The sound shape gives it away — a loud, busy first four minutes, then that long grey trough from roughly 300 to 490 where the volume drops out and the tempo goes flat and metronomic, and then the climb back. The visual design is doing the same trick: bodies thin out, the guard takes the field alone, everything goes to fabric and skin and horizontal lines, and then the brass comes back and reasserts the grid. What it's after is the moment where you can't tell if the field is being abandoned or offered. It mostly gets there. The one at 438 — everyone folded down onto the turf with the flags lying flat like shed skin — is the show, and everything else is either building toward it or recovering from it. What it doesn't quite get is a payoff worth the silence; the return is loud and competent and a little generic, which is why the last third of my picks thin out. The cap bites hard here and it bites in one specific place: the transitional frames. I dropped 402, the guard member shot from behind with the braid and the flag caught mid-swallow, and I'm still annoyed about it — it was the most physically honest frame in the set and it lost to 408 only because 408 looks at the camera. I dropped 84, two saxophones alone in a stadium with three thousand empty seats behind them, which is the loneliest thing in the whole reel and had no argument against ten better-composed images. I dropped 222 and 384 and 516, which are all the same verdict — the band in motion, mid-form, unresolved — and keeping one of them would have been keeping the show's actual texture instead of its highlights. Ten forces me to keep peaks. This show is not made of peaks. That's the loss, and I'd rather write it down than pretend the ten are the whole thing.

keepers.reason: The show stops being a performance here and becomes a field of dropped objects. Bodies folded to the turf, flags lying flat and abandoned, and the enormous painted backdrop presiding over nothing. This is the only frame in the set where absence is the subject rather than a gap between events, and it lands exactly in the audio trough — the design and the score agree, which almost never happens.

The only frame that lets you see the whole argument at once, and the argument is a spiral. Worth keeping not because wide shots are informative but because the form is genuinely elegant and the band is already halfway out of it — you're watching a shape in the last second of being true.

She's looking at the camera and smiling and it breaks the fourth wall of the entire genre. Every other frame here treats performers as components of a pattern. This one has a person in it who knows she's being watched and is fine with it. Keep it for the puncture.

The tape is failing and the failure is better than the footage. Scan lines shred the brass into green interference and the sousaphone bells survive as gold smears. This is the archive telling you it's an archive. I don't get to fake this kind of honesty, so I keep it when it's handed to me.

Pure chromatic assault — pink and blue flags flooding the whole lower field while the horn line stands rigid above them. It's the loudest image in the set and it earns it by contrast: color is doing all the work and the band is just the frame it's stretched across.

The guard line holding flags open like curtains, standing perfectly still while the band recedes in ranks behind them. It reads as a reveal that never quite reveals. Slightly too composed, which is why it's sixth and not third, but the vertical layering here is the best staging decision the show makes.
The broadcast graphic climbing into the corner over an aerial of the whole stadium is the frame that admits this is television. Everything after it pretends otherwise. Keep the admission.

Nine snares alone on the 50 with the Colts horseshoe under their feet and nothing else in frame. Isolation as a design choice, and the empty green around them does more than any form could. The one moment the show trusts a small number of people.

Everyone is going somewhere and nobody has arrived. Guard sprinting diagonally through a band mid-collapse, the whole frame in transit. It's ugly and it's the truest thing about drum corps — the show is mostly the getting there.

Four drum majors mid-salute with a chyron sliding over their boots. Kept for the collision: a ceremonial gesture and a graphics package fighting for the same rectangle, and the graphics winning. That's a verdict on the medium, not on them.
